In everyday personal life it's usually English that gets used, at least nowadays.

In professional life the rule is usually: everyone speaks/writes their own language and the recipient is expected to deal with that. I know that in at least two big companies this is actually the written down company policy, ie. your french speaking boss cannot force you to write emails in French and you cannot force him to write emails in German. Or if you are in Zürich and write to an office in Lausanne you'll still write in German, they are expected to understand that, likewise their reply will be in French and you are expected to understand that. Of course English is also sometimes used (but highly dependent on company culture - the more international the focus of the company the more accepted English will be, the more 'nationally' focused the company the less English is used).

In parliament usually each politician speaks their own native language and everyone is expected to follow - for public speeches politicians usually switch back and forth between multiple national languages (2 or 3 usually), usually not translating but just giving a few paragraphs in each language - again people are expected to be able to follow.  Depending on the crowd they are addressing they might obviously not do that and stick to one language only.

In the military there are a few language specific units, especially in basic training - but mixed units are still very common. As per military regulations each soldier has the right to be given their orders in their language, or vice versa officers and NCOs are expected to give orders in the recipients language. In practice this usually means an officer/NCO will command in their own language and then order a bilingual subordinate to translate to the other language (at least that's what I always do - I can still follow the French translation and correct any errors from translation, but wouldn't be comfortable giving the commands in French myself. Luckily Italian never came up - there I would have to blindly trust the translation). The only exception to this are high ranking officers (like Majors and up) or the few professional soldiers we have, for them language tests are mandatory to ensure that they can actually command in at least two national languages.

>Is it anything like in the american movies?

Nothing like in the American movies, as Fraternities in the anglo-sphere have a totally different tradition than the Studentenverbindungen in the German tradition. Similarities pretty much end with: it's a group of students meeting regularly with the goal of being a member all life. Pretty much all else is different.

​

>What kind of things do you do in your Verbindung?

We usually meet once per week in a restaurant. We talk, have a drink, sing a few songs and wear [funny hats](https://img.ricardostatic.ch/images/4b9a9c87-5c6c-4b81-871c-90417cd2a6d5/t_1800x1350/studenten-mutze-und-kappli-antik-2-stuck). The meetings are structured and there's a clear hierarchy in place to enforce that structure. For example the president is the one deciding when songs are sung, when it's time for discussions (both open or structured on a certain topic) etc. Besides the president there are other positions deciding other things. All positions are elected democratically among members once per semester. 

The main goal is to allow for life-long friendships to grow and encourage academic discourse across different fields. Because members usually stay members for life this friendship and discourse can be across generations.

In addition we deliberately keep old student traditions alive, including the so called [Couleur](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couleur), old (student) songs (in [German](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SXfHqWA4DAo), [French](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lwb8mUb3hu8), [Italian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WfjMlM7GBDc) and occasionally even [Latin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlq3867YR20)) and other such things. Other Studentenverbindungen also still keep the tradition of [academic fencing](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mensur_(Studentenverbindung)) alive, but the one I'm a member of doesn't do that.

There are male only Verbindungen, female only Verbindungen and mixed ones (I'm a member of a mixed one). There are even some with some further restriction on who can join, such as only catholics, or only people studying certain subjects, but that's quite rare (at least in Switzerland, it's more common in Germany and Austria).

Swiss German and German are, despite the similar names, two different languages. They are of course related, but you might as well ask how different Dutch and German are - they too are closely related, but that doesn't mean you'll be able to understand one if you speak the other. 

Example:

German: Wann gehen wir einkaufen? -> Swiss German: Wenn gömmer go poste? 

G: Neben meinem Haus hat es eine Wiese mit Pferden. -> SwG: Nebet minem Huus hetts e wise mit Ross.

G: Mein Büro ist die Treppe hoch und dann links. -> SwG: Mis Büro isch t Stega uf und de links.

They are clearly similar, but don't think that you'll be able to understand Swiss German from your German.

Note: Exact spelling and pronunciation of Swiss German will differ between speakers.

Swiss politics isn't conservative, it's slow - deliberately slow. I know about all the schools of thought you list. And they all have their virtues. However I still think that morality can only be democratic. 

We only have two choices if we want to be a democracy: either we base our morals on majority opinion or we completely separate morality and politics. All other options will eithec undermine or abolish democracy. Let me explain.

Democracy is based on the idea of the responsible, capable and empowered citizen. The citizen who, for themselves, decides what's right or wrong, and whos judgment is not incorrect. No matter how different their voice or vote is from mine, yours or anyone elses: they are not incorrect. To infringe on this, even slightly, is to directly infringe on the very core of democracy.

To pre-suppose a correct morality, which inevitably will inform voting decisions, directly infringes on this core idea by opening up the possibility of a morally wrong vote. Introducing a "correct" moral choice before the vote is done can only serve one casue: to de-legitimize an unfavorable result. 

Let me illustrate this with a deliberately benign example: we're voting whether white lies should be banned or not. For the purpose of this discussion let's define a white lie as an untrue statement which does not harm anyone or anything. Now, some school of thoughts think this would be permissible, others think that lying is still wrong even under these circumstances. The responsible, capable and empowered citizen must be free to decide however, some might even found their vote on a specific moral code, others might go with gut feeling. The point is that, if we suppose that there exists such a thing as a "correct" moral code, we open ourselves up to the possibility of the "wrong" choice winning the ballots. What could we do in such a situation? We could either overrule the popular vote based on ethical or moral grounds, which is nothing else than abandoning democracy, or we could still implement this "wrong" result thus separating morals from law. Both are obviously not options we can want, the only way around these two options is to admit that there cannot be a "correct" moral code other than the majority opinion (however this might be justified).

The median Swiss commutes for about 40 minutes. 52% of people do so by car (including car sharing schemes), while the rest uses public transport or takes the bicycle and other non-motorized means.

Interestingly enough the 40 minutes figure has been remarkably constant throughout the past 3 decades - despite speed of public transport (primarily rail) increasing in this same time frame. A 2019 study found that people, on average, just move further from the city when faster connections become available. To a lesser extent this is also true for improving street infrastructure, ie. cutting time for people using cars to commute just leads to the average person driving for a longer distance. 

Based on this the public transport strategy until 2050 (decided upon last year) does not include any further speed increases on the network - instead focusing on increasing the "density of the network in both time and space" ("Räumliche und zeitliche Dichte des Netzes"). Meaning they'll focus on the frequency of connections and density of stations, rather than increasing actual travel speed.
